source_refs.note: Book p. 52-55: 2.10 heading (no own text; the section starts with 2.10.1); our overview of the subsections

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The book prints no text under the heading 2.10 itself; the section starts directly with 2.10.1. This short overview is ours.
In 2.9 we found where a function rises and where it falls. Now we ask: where does it reach its highest and lowest values? These values are called extreme values (extrema): a maximum is a highest value, a minimum a lowest value.
Two kinds are studied: global (absolute) extrema, the highest or lowest value on the whole interval, and local (relative) extrema, the highest or lowest value only in a small neighbourhood of the point.

blocks.title: Teaching note
Teaching note
blocks.text: Why this matters: largest profit, least cost, strongest signal, shortest time are all extreme values. Section 2.14 of this unit applies these ideas to real-world problems.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Extrema = maximum and minimum values of a function.
2. Global (absolute): compared with every point of the interval. Local (relative): compared only with nearby points.
3. Extrema inside an interval occur at critical points; on a closed interval the end points must be checked too.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Confusing the point and the value: the maximum value is \(f(c)\); it occurs at \(x = c\).
2. Thinking every local maximum is the greatest value of the function: a local maximum can be lower than a local minimum elsewhere.
